response.text: Accrual accounting records income and expenses when they happen, not when money changes hands. If you send a bill to a customer, you record the sale right away under accrual—even if they pay later. If you get a bill from a supplier, you record the expense when the service or product is received, not when you pay. Cash-basis accounting waits until cash is actually received or paid. Under cash basis you only count income when the payment lands in your bank and count expenses when you pay the bill. Accrual gives a clearer picture of ongoing business activity because it matches money earned with the costs that created it. Cash basis is simpler and can show your immediate cash flow more clearly. Small businesses often start with cash basis because it’s easy, while larger or growing businesses use accrual to plan, compare across time, and meet reporting requirements.
